video_caption: The video opens with a man, presumably Vladimir Putin, in a dark suit and maroon tie, standing at a podium with two microphones, against a background of white walls and gold trim, flanked by Russian flags. This transitions to an image of a man resembling Donald Trump being held by several police officers, his face contorted. The next shot shows a young woman resembling Taylor Swift, with blonde hair, red lipstick, and braces, laughing with her mouth wide open, against a bright, hazy background. This is followed by a graphic that reads "FAKE" with letters composed of fragmented images of women, and below it, "Identify Deepfakes" with an image of a woman's face overlaid with white facial recognition points and lines. The scene then shifts to a close-up of a person's hands, adorned with multiple ornate silver rings, holding a string of green and turquoise beads. Subsequently, three distinct deepfake-like images are shown in quick succession: first, a woman with dark curly hair and bright makeup smiling against a solid green background; second, a man with a beard and short dark hair smiling broadly with a blurred green background; and third, a man with short dark hair and a black beret, with a slight smile and a blurred green background. This is followed by an image of a woman with long brown hair, wearing a dark blue textured hat and red lipstick, looking off to the right. Next, a young woman with long brown hair, wearing a black baseball cap backward and a plaid shirt under a dark jacket, smiles widely in a snowy, mountainous outdoor setting. The video then displays a close-up of an older man with white hair, smiling gently, against a blue background with a blurred American flag. A split image appears next, showing two nearly identical smiling faces of a man resembling Mark Zuckerberg, with minor differences in facial texture and lighting between the left and right sides. This is replaced by a humorous image of an orange cat nestled among golden-brown croissants. The next scene presents a surreal, stylized image of a woman in a white dress floating in a dark, stormy sky with lightning, while a large, disembodied hand reaches up from the foreground. This gives way to a highly stylized, almost cartoonish image of a man resembling Joe Biden, with exaggerated wrinkles and a tan line, eating soft-serve ice cream. The video then transitions to a screen showing a Photoshop interface, with a cityscape image being manipulated; various layers and adjustment panels are visible as the user zooms in and rotates elements. The video opens with a graphic featuring the Microsoft logo and "Microsoft AI" text next to a blue, glowing, polygonal brain model, as a male voice discusses companies investing in AI. This transitions to a young Black man working at a desk, looking at a computer screen displaying various charts and graphs, while taking notes with a pen. The scene then shifts to a block of text, resembling an email header, with phrases like "Return-Path: <m.mouse@disney.com>" (m.mouse@disney.com) and "From: "Mickey Mouse" <m.mouse@disney.com>" (Mickey Mouse), and highlighted sections for "cybercrime .org", "dmarc=none", "spf=none", and "dkim=none", with the speaker mentioning verifying emails. A person in a black t-shirt with braided hair enters a brightly lit, rustic-looking store. Inside the same store, a man in a white apron stands behind a counter, and the person from before, now in a black t-shirt, stands facing him, holding a red cloth; an Instagram notification pops up at the top of the screen reading "SURPRISE* Party" (Surprise Party) and "Sam: yo two days till the party" (Sam: two days till the party). A person with curly hair and earbuds looks directly at the camera, then down at their phone, as a search bar graphic with "Send" and "Whats the theme gonna be?" (What's the theme going to be?) appears. The scene cuts to a person vacuuming a room with a red couch, and another Instagram notification appears: "*SURPRISE* Party" (Surprise Party) and "Max: What's the theme gonna be??" (Max: What's the theme going to be?). A person in a yellow shirt sits on a red couch, looking sad. An Instagram chat screen shows an image of a group of diverse young people outside a house, with a text bubble below it saying "she loooves snails lmao". A person in a white tank top and earbuds stands on a running track, looking at their phone. The interior of the rustic store is shown again, with a person behind the counter and the woman from before holding a colorful, snail-shaped object. The exterior of the same store is shown at dusk, with a "SAM'S BBQ" (Sam's BBQ) sign and a neon "OPEN" sign; a woman walks away from the store pushing a bicycle. A young man with short curly hair smiles directly at the camera. A young Black woman in a black t-shirt is seen in what appears to be a subway car, holding a green snail-shaped piñata. The woman stands next to her bicycle outside the store, and an Instagram poll graphic appears asking "NAME THE SNAIL!!!" (NAME THE SNAIL!!!) with options "Speedy !!" and "Shelly !!" (Shelly !!). The text "The Send Off" appears over the same shot of the woman with the bicycle and piñata outside the store. A red car is parked on a dirt road, with several cardboard boxes behind it, and two people are interacting near the car. The screen goes black, then a white text bubble appears on a black background saying "where is everyone? 😟" (where is everyone? 😟). The video concludes with three people sitting on the ground in a backyard, playing with crafts and eating snacks, against a white and purple fence with red and white paint.

The video opens with a close-up shot of numerous circular "VOTE" buttons. These buttons feature a design inspired by the American flag, with red and white stripes on the bottom half, white stars on a blue background on the top right, and the word "VOTE" prominently displayed in black capital letters on the white section. The buttons are piled on top of each other, creating a textured background. This scene transitions to a screenshot of a news article. The article's headline reads, "The White House wants to 'cryptographically verify' videos of Joe Biden so viewers don't mistake them for deepfakes." (The White House wants to 'cryptographically verify' videos of Joe Biden so viewers don't mistake them for deepfakes). The article, dated Feb 8, 2024, and attributed to Kali Haas, details the White House's intention to implement cryptographic verification for President Biden's videos to combat the spread of deepfake misinformation. Below the main image, a caption states, "Biden's AI advisor, Ben Buchanan, said a way to verify White House releases is "in the works."" Accompanying the text is a photograph of President Joe Biden, taken outdoors, where he is seen wearing dark sunglasses and a suit. He is smiling and waving his right hand towards the camera, with a wooden swingset and trees visible in the background.

The video displays a static screenshot of a news article titled "The White House wants to 'cryptographically' verify videos of Joe Biden so viewers don't mistake them for deepfakes." The article is authored by Kaili Hays and dated February 8, 2024, 5:03 PM EST. Below the title, a photograph of President Joe Biden is featured, where he is seen outdoors, wearing dark sunglasses, a dark suit, a light blue shirt, and a dark tie, smiling and waving with his right hand. The background consists of blurred greenery and what appears to be part of a red-brown wooden structure, possibly a swingset or fence. A caption beneath the image identifies him as "President Joe Biden. Drew Angerer/Getty Images." Further down, a bullet point reads: "Biden's AI advisor, Ben Buchanan, said a way to verify White House releases is "in the works."" The overall screen has a white background with black text.

The video segment transitions through several screens illustrating the application of public/private key pairs. It begins with a white webpage titled "GnuPG" (The GNU Privacy Guard), detailing its use for encrypting, signing data, and verifying communications and software packages. The text highlights its role as a "complete and free implementation of the OpenPGP standard." This transitions to a "www.based.win" shopping website featuring t-shirts, overlaid with a "Certificate Viewer" pop-up displaying the website's verified certificate information, including "Issued To: Common Name (CN): www.based.win." Next, a webpage from "Whonix" is shown, featuring download options and instructions under "Verify the Whonix KVM images" that mention "OpenPGP" and "signify," demonstrating software package verification. This then changes to a close-up of three golden Bitcoin coins with the "B" logo, positioned in front of a blurred background of financial charts, representing cryptocurrency transactions. Finally, a person wearing a dark blue shirt types on a silver laptop, while holographic images of documents with checkboxes and a signature field are projected above. The person uses a digital pen to virtually sign one of these documents, illustrating the cryptographic signing of various file types, including archives.

The video displays a static screenshot of a news article. In the upper left corner, the category "TECH" is visible. The main headline reads: "The White House wants to 'cryptographically' verify videos of Joe Biden so viewers don't mistake them for deepfakes." Below this, the author and date are listed: "Kaelen Haas | Feb 8, 2024, 5:02 PM EST". The central part of the screen features a photograph of President Joe Biden. He is shown outdoors, wearing a dark suit, a light blue shirt, and dark sunglasses. He is smiling faintly and waving with his right hand. The background behind him is blurred, showing trees and a red metal swing set or playground structure. Beneath the image, it states: "President Joe Biden. Drew Angerer/Getty Images" (Image credit). Further down, a bullet point provides additional information: "Biden's AI advisor, Ben Buchanan, said a way to verify White House releases is 'in the works.'" The overall background of the screen is white.

The video begins with a screenshot of a news article titled "The White House wants to 'cryptographically' verify' videos of Joe Biden so viewers don't mistake them for deepfakes." Below the headline, an image shows President Joe Biden outdoors, wearing sunglasses and a dark suit, smiling and waving, with a blurred green and red background. The article credits Drew Angerer/Getty Images for the photo and includes a bullet point stating, "Biden's AI advisor, Ben Buchanan, said a way to verify White House releases is 'in the works.'" The scene then quickly transitions to a clip of rapper Eminem dancing energetically in a grey and white tracksuit against a dark background with a large yellow 'E' logo, accompanied by the text "AS THE DOCTORS RUSH TO SAVE SHADY...". This is followed by a clip of singer Miley Cyrus in white underwear and a crop top, sitting on a large grey wrecking ball, holding its chain, in a concrete room with broken walls. The video then shifts to a series of screenshots depicting different digital storefronts. First, the Microsoft Store homepage is shown, featuring various app and game tiles like "Anime Month," "Valentine's Day," "Join PC Game Pass," and "Microsoft 365," along with essential apps such as "TikTok" and "Adobe Acrobat Reader DC." Next, the Google Play Store (Games section) appears, displaying promotional banners for Valentine's Day, "Star Trek" and other games like "Candy Crush Saga" and "PUBG Mobile." Finally, the Apple App Store website is presented, initially showing a collage of app icons and a large logo with the tagline "The apps you love. From a place you can trust." The view then scrolls down, revealing various sections detailing the App Store's features, security measures ("100% of apps are automatically screened for known malware"), privacy policies, and content moderation efforts, including statistics about rejected submissions and removed apps. The scrolling text also highlights "Hardware and software. Powering amazing experiences together by design." and "Over 900K apps have secure payment technologies like Apple Pay." The final transition shows the SourceForge website, an open-source software repository. The screen displays a "Browse Open Source Software" page with filter options for OS, Category, License, Translations, Programming Language, and Status, and lists numerous open-source projects like "Apache OpenOffice," "XAMPP," "qBittorrent," and "CrystalDiskInfo," as the page scrolls through the listings.

The video segment begins by displaying a computer screen showing the SourceForge website, featuring software listings for "Shotcut," "libjpeg-turbo," and "Rufus," complete with descriptions, star ratings, download statistics, and project links. At the 0:01 mark, the screen transitions to a black background, and two identical "Error" pop-up windows appear, each stating, "Click 'Fix' to fix error," with a "Fix" button. These pop-ups rapidly multiply and overlap, filling the screen chaotically. By 0:03, the style of the pop-up windows changes to a more classic blue title bar design, with one central pop-up displaying "C:\WINDOWS\system32\taskmgr.exe" (English: The service did not respond to the start or control request in a timely fashion.) and an "OK" button, while numerous other blue-barred error messages, such as "Windows Update Standalone Installer" (English: Installer encountered an error: 0x80070424 The specified service does not exist as an installed service.) and "System Restore encountered an error," continue to accumulate, some appearing skewed and rotated. As the video progresses, the screen becomes entirely overwhelmed by a dense, chaotic array of various error pop-up windows, some with red "X" icons, and text related to "Services" (English: Windows could not start the Windows Search service on Local Computer. Error 2: The system cannot find the file specified.), suggesting a system-wide failure or virus infection. The visual composition then transforms into a highly distorted and glitched display dominated by blue and pink/magenta colors, with pronounced scanlines and artifacting, depicting a complete visual breakdown of the operating system.

The video displays a static computer screen showing the Google Play Store page for the game "Candy Crush Saga." The page features the game's title in large text, followed by the developer "King," and information such as "Contains ads, In-app purchases," a "4.6" star rating from "37 M reviews," "1B+ Downloads," and content ratings including "Everyone 10+" and "Editors' Choice." A prominent green "Install" button is centered on the left side of the screen, with smaller "Share" and "Add to wishlist" buttons below it. To the right, a large video player continuously showcases dynamic gameplay footage of "Candy Crush Saga," featuring colorful candy matching puzzles. Below this video player, four smaller static image previews of the game are displayed, labeled "Explore the Candy World," "Match Candy Combos!", "Thousands of Puzzling Challenges!", and "Smash the Chocolate!". On the far right, a sidebar shows "App support" and "More by King," listing "Candy Crush Soda Saga" and "Farm Heroes Saga."

A brief shot of a crowd of people gathered outdoors on a street is shown, and the segment concludes with a red-hued animation of multiple virus particles, resembling coronaviruses, floating against a dark red background.

The video opens with a screenshot of a news article from Kali Hays, dated February 8, 2024, titled "The White House wants to 'cryptographically verify' videos of Joe Biden so viewers don't mistake them for deepfakes." (The title indicates the US White House aims to use cryptographic methods to authenticate videos of President Joe Biden, preventing them from being confused with AI-generated deepfakes). An accompanying image shows President Joe Biden, wearing sunglasses and a dark suit over a light blue shirt, waving with his right hand in an outdoor setting, with reddish-brown playground equipment in the blurred background. Below the image, it's captioned "President Joe Biden. Drew Angerer/Getty Images." A bullet point below the image states, "Biden's AI advisor, Ben Buchanan, said a way to verify White House releases is 'in the works.'" The scene then transitions to a webpage titled "GnuPG," featuring the main heading "The GNU Privacy Guard." The page describes GnuPG as a free, complete implementation of the OpenPGP standard, highlighting its use for encrypting and signing data and communications, and mentioning its availability as free software. It also includes a section titled "RECONQUER YOUR PRIVACY" which discusses the importance of encryption and privacy, quoting Edward Snowden. The screen then transitions back to the initial news article about Joe Biden and deepfakes.
